extracted.intended_audience: upper-level undergraduate / beginning graduate students in complex analysis; instructors and readers studying residues, Laurent series, and several-complex-variable holomorphicity
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, definitions, and proof-sketches for global complex-analysis results: Cauchy Integral Theorem in homology form, the Residue Theorem, Laurent series expansions (existence/uniqueness), treatment of isolated/essential singularities, and holomorphic functions in several variables (power-series characterization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: simply connected (standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pathwise connected metric space X (e.g., a bounded region U) is simply connected in the standard sense if every loop γ(t) (t in [a,b]) based at a point p of X is homotopic to a constant loop. A loop is a path γ with γ(a)=γ(b)=p; homotopy is a continuous f:[a,b]×[0,1]→X with f(t,0)=γ(t), f(t,1)=σ(t) and f(a,s)=f(b,s)=p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains loop, based, homotopic, and constant loop; intuition: loops that can be continuously deformed to the constant loop. Used to relate winding numbers and homotopy; choice of base point irrelevant because loops based at different points are related by a path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winding numbers ↔ homotopy criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For a loop γ in U based at p and fixed z0 in C\U, the winding number n(γ,z0) (defined by the integral (1/2πi)∮γ dz/(z−z0)) is 0 if and only if γ is homotopic to a constant loop. Nonzero winding number implies γ is not homotopic to constant in C\{z0}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the lift-argument (lifting arg values to iR) and a discussion showing how winding number zero equates to the lifted argument change being zero. Notes the converse is more subtle and connects to the Riemann Mapping Theorem: if all winding numbers are 0 the region is conformally a disk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: boundary cycle (homologous to 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: A piecewise C^1 cycle Γ in a bounded region U is a boundary cycle if n(Γ,a)=0 for every a in C\U. (Ahlfors calls these cycles 'homologous to 0'.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to restrict cycles for which global Cauchy-type theorems hold in non-simply-connected regions. Note: a cycle decomposed into piecewise C^1 closed curves may have constituents that are not boundary cycles (warning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem B.45: Cauchy Integral Theorem (homology form)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in a bounded region U in C, then ∮_Γ f(z) dz = 0 for every piecewise C^1 boundary cycle Γ in U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: reduces to the usual Cauchy theorem when U is simply connected (every cycle is a boundary cycle). Proof strategy: prove special polygonal case using rectangle decomposition and Goursat; then approximate general piecewise C^1 boundary cycles by polygonal cycles inside U and use decomposition + Cauchy in disks. Emphasizes the role of winding numbers n(Γ,a) and integers combinations of rectangle integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning about decomposition of boundary cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: Although any cycle can be written as a combination of piecewise C^1 closed curves, the constituent piecewise C^1 closed curves of a boundary cycle need not themselves be boundary cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution when applying decomposition arguments: integrals over subcurves may not individually vanish even when the full boundary cycle integral vanishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary B.46: Residue Theorem (boundary-cycle form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f be analytic in a region U except for poles at points {z_j}. If Γ is a piecewise C^1 boundary cycle in U not passing through any poles, then ∮_Γ f(z) dz = 2πi Σ_j Res f(z_j) · n(Γ,z_j), with only finitely many nonzero terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from the Cauchy Integral Theorem (Theorem B.44). Formula includes winding numbers n(Γ,z_j) as integer multiplicities. Applicable to cycles homologous to zero in complement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem B.47: Laurent series in an annulus (existence & uniqueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in the annulus {z: R1 < |z−z0| < R2}, then there exist unique g1 analytic for |z−z0| < R2 and g2 analytic for |z−z0| > R1 that vanishes at infinity, such that f(z) = g1(z) + g2(z). Moreover, writing An = (1/2πi)∮_C f(ζ)(ζ−z0)^{−n−1} dζ, one has the Laurent expansion f(z) = Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} An (z−z0)^n converging in the annulus; g1 is the power-series (nonnegative n) part and g2 is the negative-power part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives explicit contour-integral formulas for coefficients An, describes domains of convergence: power series part converges for |z−z0|<R2, negative-power part in |z−z0|>R1 (with vanishing at infinity), and uniform convergence on closed subannuli. Uniqueness proven via Liouville: difference would be entire and vanish at infinity. The proof constructs g1 and g2 via contour integrals on two circles and uses homology (C2−C1 is a boundary cycle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulas and computation of Laurent coefficients (An)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any r with R1 < r < R2 and C the circle |ζ−z0|=r, An = (1/2πi)∮_C f(ζ)(ζ−z0)^{−n−1} dζ for all integer n (−∞<n<∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how to derive coefficients for both positive and negative indices by appropriate contour choices and change of variables. Provides Fubini/Taylor interchanges used to justify expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary B.48: decomposition at an isolated singularity
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in a region U except possibly for an isolated singularity at z0∈U, then f(z) = g(z) + h((z−z0)^{−1}) where g is analytic on U, h is analytic on all of C with h(0)=0, and the term h((z−z0)^{−1}) is the singular part built from negative powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specializes Theorem B.47 to R1=0 to separate principal (singular) part and analytic part. If the singularity is a pole, h is a polynomial; for essential singularities h is an entire function with nontrivial negative-power series. This decomposition allows the extension of residue-style theorems to general isolated singularities but warns that usual derivative formulas for residues may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary B.49: Residue Theorem for isolated singularities (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f be analytic in U except for isolated singularities {z_j}. If Γ is a piecewise C^1 boundary cycle in U not passing through any singularities, then ∮_Γ f(z) dz = 2πi Σ_j Res f(z_j) n(Γ,z_j), with only finitely many nonzero terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement holds but the usual formulas for residues in terms of derivatives (e.g., for poles) may not apply for essential singularities; thus this general form is of theoretical interest but less useful computationally. The Argument Principle can fail in presence of essential singularities—examples illustrate unexpected integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution / example: essential singularities break usual residue/argument intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: f(z)=e^{1/z} and g(z)=sin(1/z) have essential singularities at 0. Behavior of integrals like ∮ f'(z)/f(z) dz or ∮ g'(z)/g(z) dz around unit circle are not governed by simple counts of zeros/poles as in the pole-only case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that integrals involving logarithmic derivatives can yield unintuitive nonzero values even when pole/zero counting would suggest otherwise; underscores need for care when extending finite-pole arguments to essential singularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: holomorphic function on open U⊆C^n
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f:U→C on an open subset U of C^n is holomorphic if it is continuous and each restriction z_j ↦ f(c1,...,cj−1,z_j,cj+1,...,cn) is analytic (in one complex variable) on each connected component of its domain — i.e., analytic in each variable separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: holomorphic ⇔ analytic in each variable and continuous; this condition implies C^∞ regularity and the Cauchy–Riemann equations in each variable. (Remark: continuity assumption can be dropped by Hartogs's Theorem.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-index notation and polydisk definition (setup for power series)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multi-index α=(α1,...,αn) with |α|=α1+...+αn, α!=α1!...αn!. Open polydisk 1(a,r) = product over j of {z_j: |z_j−a_j|<r_j}. Closed polydisk 1(a,r)̄ has |z_j−a_j|≤r_j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to index multivariable Taylor/Laurent expansions and to state radius/convergence regions for power series in several complex variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem B.50 (Osgood's Lemma): power-series characterization of holomorphic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is holomorphic on an open set U⊆C^n and 1(a,r)⊂U is an open polydisk, then f has an absolutely convergent power series expansion f(z)=Σ_{α} c_α (z−a)^α valid on 1(a,r), with uniform convergence on compact subsets; f is C^∞ and c_α = (D^α f)(a)/α!. Conversely, if every point p∈U has some polydisk where f admits an absolutely convergent power series, then f is holomorphic on U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via iterated Cauchy integral formulas in each variable and geometric-series expansion; Fubini justifies interchanging sums and integrals. Consequences: termwise differentiation is valid; coefficients are given by iterated contour integrals; regularity (C^∞) and analytic-in-each-variable equivalence follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for differentiation and coefficient formulas in several variables
rubrics_metrics.description: The power series for a holomorphic function in a polydisk can be differentiated term-by-term; D^α f at the center equals α! c_α. Uniform convergence on compacta allows interchange of differentiation and summation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the computational recipe for coefficients via (2πi)^{-n} iterated contour integrals of f over the polydisk product circles, and justifies smoothness and termwise operations using Theorem 1.23 and Fubini.
